preamble: The change of the voiced alveolar fricative [z] to a rhotic [r] is the core step of historical rhotacism. It usually affects intervocalic or word-final [z], which itself often comes from earlier voiced [s]. Northwest Germanic, Latin and Umbrian all show it, and Oghur Turkic r corresponds regularly to Common Turkic z.

languageExamples.language: Old English / Old High German (vs. Gothic)

examples.to: Old English māra, Old High German mēro
examples.note: Proto-Germanic *z (from *s by Verner's law) became Proto-West Germanic *ʀ (*maiʀō) and then r; Gothic keeps z.

examples.to: Old English hord, Old High German hort
examples.note: Via Proto-West Germanic *hoʀd; the alternation also survives in English was/were and German verlieren/verloren.
Runic inscriptions show the intermediate ʀ; North Germanic merged it with r later than West Germanic.

examples.to: Classical Latin flōrem (gen. flōris; nom. flōs keeps s)
examples.note: Intervocalic *s was voiced to [z] and then became r in the 4th century BC; word-final s did not change.
Varro (De lingua Latina VII.26) records that in many words the ancients said s where later speakers said r.
Oscan kept intervocalic s as voiced [z], while Umbrian took it on to r, like Latin -ārum. Late Umbrian also turned final -s into -r.

Oghur (Bulgar) Turkic r corresponds to Common Turkic z. On the rhotacism account Common Turkic z is original; the competing account reconstructs Proto-Turkic *ŕ, with Common Turkic z as the innovation.

sources: Fortson, B. W. (2010). Indo-European Language and Culture: An Introduction (2nd ed.). Wiley-Blackwell. https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Indo-European+Language+and+Culture%3A+An+Introduction%2C+2nd+Edition-p-9781405188968
